origin_region: Mie · Yokkaichi and Suzuka (Ise); also Kyoto, Nara, Fukuoka
processing: Bushes are covered with shade cloth for roughly 7–14 days before picking, often with the cloth draped directly over the rows, then the leaf is steamed, rolled and dried as sencha.
harvest_season: First flush (late April–May); second-flush kabusecha exists for cheaper grades but is not the point.
appearance_dry: Dark green needles, finer and darker than ordinary sencha but not as black-green as gyokuro.
taste_profile: Rounder and more savoury than sencha, with a gentle seaweed umami, mild sweetness and softened astringency, while keeping some of sencha's freshness.

brewing.notes: Between sencha and gyokuro: a little more leaf, cooler water (60–70 °C) and a longer first steep. Works beautifully cold-brewed overnight at about 1 g per 100 ml.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's first flush, usually labelled kabusecha or 'kabuse sencha' with the prefecture; Mie lots are often sold under the Ise-cha name. It appears in shops from late spring and, like sencha, is meant to be finished within the year; a few producers rest it for a couple of months like gyokuro, but there is no tradition of ageing it.
description:
Kabusecha, 'covered tea', sits halfway between sencha and gyokuro: shaded for a week or two rather than three, usually with cloth draped straight over the bushes instead of hung on frames. Mie prefecture, whose tea is sold under the Ise-cha name, makes more of it than anywhere else, with Kyoto, Nara and Fukuoka behind.

A shorter shade gives a partial version of the gyokuro effect. The leaf keeps more theanine and makes more chlorophyll than an unshaded one, so the needles are darker and the cup is rounder and more savoury, but it also keeps the freshness and lift of sencha. Processing is standard: steam, roll, dry, refine. In practice the boundary is blurry; some of the best 'sencha' from Kyoto and Kagoshima is shaded for a few days before picking, and whether a tea is sold as sencha or kabusecha is partly a labelling decision.

Brewed at 60–70 °C with a slightly longer first steep it gives a sweet, seaweed-savoury cup with a soft texture and only a hint of grip; brewed hotter like sencha it is still perfectly good, just grassier and less umami. Cold-brewed overnight at about 1 g per 100 ml it is one of the best Japanese teas there is. For anyone who finds gyokuro too intense or too expensive, kabusecha is the sensible introduction to shaded tea.

It is labelled kabusecha or 'kabuse sencha' with the prefecture, and it is good value for the umami you get, typically priced a little above sencha and well below gyokuro. Watch for the two mislabels: 'gyokuro' that was shaded for only a week, and 'kabuse' used loosely for anything that saw a bit of shade. Mie's lots are often deep-steamed as well as shaded, which makes a thick, sweet, cloudy tea; Kyoto and Fukuoka lots tend to be lighter and clearer.

If you buy only one umami-style tea for everyday drinking, make it this one.
